Several commentators, such as al-Jaza'iri and al-Qasimi, hold that the purpose is to magnify God and bring His greatness within human understanding, without detailing the nature of the Throne.

This verse states that on the Day of Judgment people will be presented before God for reckoning and recompense, and that nothing of their deeds or secrets will be hidden from Him. The commentators agree on the core meaning: God's knowledge encompasses everything. The word 'ard' (presentation) means the settling of accounts, likened to a ruler reviewing his troops to learn their condition. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relay, through Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn Mas'ud, a hadith describing three presentations: two marked by argument and excuses, and a third in which the scrolls fly in hands, one person taking his record in the right hand and another in the left. Al-Razi repeats this account and adds that the true inner state of each person will become known. As to the phrase 'nothing will be hidden', Ibn 'Abbas and al-Baghawi take it to mean that no hidden act remains concealed, while Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As sees it as the distinction between believer and unbeliever, and between the righteous and the wicked. Others, such as al-Zamakhshari, understand that even nakedness will not be covered, since people will be gathered bare. Al-Tabari prefers the feminine reading, according to which the hidden matter is something concealed in worldly life. On recitation, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb with a ya, while the majority read it with a ta, for the feminine noun. Ibn al-Qayyim links the verse to the hadith on the hard reckoning and cites ʿUmar's advice to take account of oneself before being judged.

This verse describes the one who receives his record of deeds in his right hand on the Day of Reckoning. He rejoices so greatly that he calls on those present to read his book, for he knows it contains good and safety. The commentators explain that receiving the book in the right hand is a sign of salvation, and that his words express confidence in his safety and joy at his deliverance. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, like most exegetes, take hā'umu to mean 'take' or 'come here', while al-Kisa'i considers it a sound that conveys the sense of seizing. As for 'inni zanantu', Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Dahhak read it as certainty, since assumption about the hereafter is certainty, whereas al-Hasan holds that the believer thought well of his Lord and so acted well. All agree that the pleasant life is a pleasing one, that the Garden is high, and that its clusters hang near, reachable whether standing, sitting or reclining, and that the people there are told to eat and drink with ease in return for the righteous deeds sent forward in the days gone by. They differ on the grammatical role of the final hā' in 'kitabiyah' and 'hisabiyah': the Basrans make 'iqra'u' govern it, the Kufans make 'hā'umu' govern it. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan treat the final hā' as a pause marker and discuss its pronunciation in continuous recitation. Muqatil and al-Dahhak report that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Asad.

This verse describes the one who is given his record in his right hand on the Day of Resurrection: he joyfully calls out to those around him to come and read his book, and then explains his joy by saying that he had been certain in worldly life that he would meet his reckoning. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Mujahid interpret the word zanantu here as certainty; al-Dahhak holds that every zann in the Qur'an from a believer is certainty and from an unbeliever is doubt, while Mujahid distinguishes the zann about the Hereafter, which is certainty, from that about this world, which is doubt. Al-Hasan al-Basri says that the believer thought well of his Lord and so acted well, while the hypocrite thought ill of Him and so acted ill. Ibn Qutayba and al-Zamakhshari hold that the verb carries the sense of knowing, because a strong supposition takes the place of knowledge in customs and rulings, whereas al-Razi and al-Nasafi explain that belief in the Hereafter is never free of passing thoughts, which is why the word for supposition is used; al-Alusi also allows the literal sense of hoping for an easy reckoning. Grammarians differ over the governing word of kitabiyah: the Kufans attach it to hā'umu, the Basrans to iqra'u. Readers keep the final ha' in pause and in connected speech following the written text of the Qur'an, while Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub drop it when connected. Ra-diya is read as pleasing or as possessing contentment. The person lives a pleasing life in an elevated garden whose fruits are within reach, and it is said to them: eat and drink with delight, for what you sent ahead of you in the days that have passed.

This verse describes the state of the one who is given his record in his right hand on the Day of Resurrection: he rejoices at his salvation and says to those around him, take and read my record. Most commentators understand the word ẓann here as certain knowledge. Ibn Zayd and Qatada say that the believer's assumption is a certainty, and al-Hasan explains that the believer thought well of his Lord and therefore acted well. As for the phrase he is in a pleasing life, the commentators agree that it means a life that is pleasing, one its owner is content with. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' read it as pleasing, while others take it as having contentment, like the Arabic forms meaning one who possesses milk or dates. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that attributing contentment to the life is a figure of speech, since its real owner is the one who lives it. Most exegetes describe this life as an endless bliss without death, sickness or old age, citing Abu Hurayra and Abu Sa'id. They also agree that the garden is high in rank and place, and that its fruits are within reach whether one stands, sits or lies down. It will be said to them: eat and drink with ease for what you sent forward in the past days, meaning the good deeds done in the world. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr take these days to be the days of fasting. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur stress that this reward is a bounty from God and not owed to deeds alone, while al-Razi links it to the causal role of action. None of the commentators settles the differences between these readings.

This passage describes the state of the one who is given his record in his right hand on the Day of Resurrection. He will be in a pleasing life, meaning a life that its owner finds agreeable, in a lofty garden, whose fruits hang near and can be picked standing, sitting or reclining, as he wishes. The commentators report that he will be told to eat and drink with pleasure and without any hardship, as a reward for the good deeds he sent ahead in the days that have passed of his earthly life. The exegetes agree that the loftiness of the garden is literal, since it lies above the heavens, and that it also means the height of its ranks and the grandeur of its dwellings. They also agree that hanî means food and drink free of any disturbance. They differ on the meaning of the phrase I thought: al-Dahhak, Mujahid and al-Hasan take it to mean certainty, while al-Hasan links it to whether one thinks well or badly of one's Lord. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr understand the past days as the days of fasting, whereas most commentators extend the sense to all righteous deeds, the view preferred by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi. As for the word radiya, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' read it as meaning well-pleasing, while al-Zamakhshari sees a figurative attribution to the life. On recitation, most readers keep the final hâ of kitabiyah and hisabiyah in line with the written mushaf, while Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub drop it when joined to what follows.

The verse describes the fruits of Paradise, qutufuha daniya, meaning their clusters are near and easy to reach. Al-Tabari, citing al-Bara' ibn Azib and Qatada, reports that a person can pick them while standing, sitting or lying down, with neither distance nor thorns preventing him. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi transmit the same explanation, while Abu Hayyan, al-Shawkani and al-Alusi stress the ease of reaching them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy take qutuf to mean the clusters or produce gathered from the trees, and Ibn Atiyya adds that the fruit comes to the one who wishes to eat it. Al-Mawardi offers a further reading in which nearness refers to ripeness, the fruit never being late.

The commentators agree that this description belongs to the account of the one who receives his record in his right hand. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that a pleasing life (radiya) means a life that is well pleasing, and that the Garden is high in rank and in place. The words "Eat and drink with pleasure" are, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi, a address to the blessed in return for their deeds in the days gone by, that is, the life of this world.

Disagreements centre on the meaning of "the days that are past" and of "what you sent forward". Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand these as the days of worldly life and the good works done in them, while Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and al-Kalbi take them to mean fasting. Al-Razi, who records this view, argues that the reward is tied to the action performed. Ibn Sa'di notes that these deeds include prayer, charity and kindness to others, and that Paradise is their fruit.

This verse describes the joy of the one who is given his record in his right hand on the Day of Judgment: he and his companions are told to eat and drink with pleasure, without any harm, as a reward for the good deeds they sent ahead in the days that have passed, meaning the days of worldly life. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that 'hanian' means free of any discomfort, so the people of Paradise suffer no harm from what they eat or drink and need neither excrement nor urine. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, take 'the days that have passed' to mean the days of worldly life. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur prefer a general meaning covering all good deeds. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Waki' and 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Rafi' say the reference is to the days of fasting, a view also given by al-Mawardi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani, and which al-Qurtubi attributes to Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the general sense is more appropriate. Al-Razi explains that 'aslafa' means to send ahead what will benefit you, and that the verse shows deeds to be the cause of reward. Some scholars, al-Razi among them, hold that 'eat' is not a binding command, since the Hereafter is not a place of obligation, while others see it as a recommendation meant to gladden the heart.

This verse describes the state of the one who is given his record in his left hand. Seeing the ugliness of his deeds, he laments and wishes he had never been given his record or known his reckoning. He also wishes that the death he suffered in this world had been the final one, with no resurrection after it. Commentators differ on the reference of "would that it had been". Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Zayd take it as a wish for death, which was the thing he most hated in the world, while Dahhak and Muhammad ibn Ka'b understand it as a death with no life after it. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi suggest the pronoun may instead refer to the state he now witnesses, which he finds more bitter than death itself. Regarding "my wealth has not availed me", Ibn 'Atiyya allows either a plain negation or a rhetorical question of rebuke, and al-Mawardi explains that his wealth in the world did not protect him. As for "my authority has perished", Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak take it to mean his argument has gone, while Ibn Zayd takes it as the loss of his worldly rule. Some report that the verse concerns Abu Jahl or al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur note that it addresses the disbelievers, and al-Razi argues that this inner torment is harsher than physical punishment.

This verse describes the state of the one who receives his record in his left hand: he wishes he had never been given his book and had not known his reckoning, regretting what he sees in it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "Would that it had been the decisive death" is a wish for a death that would end everything with no resurrection afterwards, and some add that he would rather die than endure what he faces. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur also allow that the pronoun may refer to the present condition, which he finds more bitter than death. As for "and I did not know what my reckoning was," al-Tabari and al-Razi take it to mean that he gains nothing from the reckoning, which falls entirely upon him, while Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as not knowing the reality of what he will be asked. Al-Mawardi suggests either that he had thought his sins few but finds them many, or that he is shocked by the severity of the punishment. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, explain "my authority has perished" as the loss of his arguments, while Ibn Zayd understands it as the loss of worldly rule and power. The final hā' in "kitabiyah" and "hisabiyah" is, according to most, a pausal hā' whose presence in continuous reading is a matter of recitation rather than meaning.

This passage describes the one who receives his record in his left hand on the Day of Judgment: he laments, wishes he had never been given his record nor known his reckoning, and wishes that his worldly death had been the final death, with no resurrection after it. The commentators agree that the pronoun in "O would that it had been" refers to death. Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain that he wished for death, since nothing was more hateful to him in this world; al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi understood it as a death with no life after it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report both meanings. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan propose another reading: the pronoun may refer to the state he sees in his record, which he finds more bitter than death itself, so he wishes that this state had been the death that finished him. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the phrase is a concise expression of regret. As for "al-qadiya", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean what cuts off life, while al-Razi sees the idea of completion and cessation. The commentators therefore agree on the core meaning: intense regret and a wish that everything would end in death, without resurrection or reckoning.

This verse describes the anguish of the one who receives his record in his left hand on the Day of Judgement. He wishes he had never been given his book and never known his reckoning, and he wishes that his death in this world had been the final one, with no resurrection after it. Then he admits that his wealth did not avail him and that his authority has vanished. The commentators broadly agree on this reading. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the "decisive death" means a death with no life after it, according to ad-Dahhak, while Qatada understood it as a wish for death, since death was the thing he hated most in the world.

On the meaning of "authority" (sultan), Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, as-Suddi and ad-Dahhak take it to mean the proof he used to argue in this life, whereas Ibn Zayd takes it to mean kingship and worldly power. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan prefer the first, broader sense, since the left-hand record concerns anyone destined for misery, not only rulers. Al-Razi sets out both views without deciding between them.

As for whether the book is given before or after entry into the Fire, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy report differing views. Abu Hayyan notes that the believer who sins may receive his book in the right hand together with those who are saved, which comforts him during his punishment. The commentators also note that among the Arabs the left hand was a sign of shame.

This passage describes the state of the one who will be given his record in his left hand on the Day of Resurrection. He laments and wishes he had never been given his book or learned his reckoning, and he wishes that his death in this world had been the final one, with no resurrection. On the phrase "my authority has perished from me," the commentators offer two main readings. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Dahhak and as-Suddi, followed by most exegetes, take it to mean that his proof has vanished and he has no argument left to plead. Ibn Zayd understands it as his worldly kingship and power, Qatada as his mastery over himself and his limbs, which he misused by disobeying, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas as the authority he held over his followers. All agree that his wealth and power avail him nothing, and then describe the punishment that follows: he is seized, his hand is chained to his neck, and he is cast into the blazing Fire.

Regarding the chain whose length is seventy cubits, all stress its terrifying extent, but they differ on how he is threaded onto it. Ibn Abbas, Sufyan, Muqatil and al-Dahhak say it enters through his rear and exits through his mouth or nostrils, while others say it enters through the mouth and exits through the rear. Al-Kalbi compares it to a thread passed through pearls. On the length of the cubit, Nawf al-Bakali reports that each cubit is seventy spans, al-Hasan says only God knows which cubit is meant, and al-Razi holds that the number seventy conveys great length rather than an exact measure.

The commentators agree that the reason for this punishment is disbelief in God together with stinginess, that is, failing to urge the feeding of the poor. They also agree on the food of the damned, al-ghislin, which Ibn Abbas identifies as the pus of the people of the Fire, while al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' describe it as a tree in Hell. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir take "hamim" here to mean a close relative who might help, without this altering the verse's core meaning.

God commands the guardians of Hell to seize this disbeliever, put a collar of chains on his neck, and cast him into the Blazing Fire to burn there. The commentators agree that the punishment is for his disbelief in the Mighty God. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that the Blazing Fire here means the greatest fire, since this man was arrogant and domineering over people. Al-Sam'ani says the binding joins the hand to the neck, and Ibn Kathir adds that a vast number of angels rush to carry out the order. On the chain of seventy cubits, the commentators differ. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi cite Ibn Abbas, who takes the cubit to be the king's cubit, and Nawf al-Bakali, who says each cubit is seventy spans. Al-Hasan leaves the exact measure to God, while Ibn Juzayy reads the number as a way of describing great length. On how the chain is threaded, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that it enters at the back and comes out through the nostrils or mouth, while others reverse this; al-Tabari also cites the Arabic idiom 'I put my head into the cap'. The verses then give the reason for this punishment: disbelief and refusal to feed the poor. The word ghislin is explained by Ibn Abbas as the pus of the damned, by Qatada as the worst food, and by al-Dahhak and al-Rabi as a tree in Hell, while al-Zamakhshari takes it as the drainage from the bodies of the damned.

The plain meaning of the verse is that God commands the guardians of Hell, after seizing this arrogant disbeliever and chaining his hand to his neck, to cast him into the Jahim, the blazing fire. The commentators explain that Jahim refers to the great fire, and that the word then placed after the shackling signals an escalation in severity rather than a long delay. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, treat the verse as part of the description of the fate of the one given his record in his left hand, punished because he did not believe in the Mighty God and did not urge the feeding of the poor. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that this fire was reserved for him because he was a tyrant who magnified himself over people, whereas Abu Hayyan judges that the word sultan here means his argument, which he considers the stronger reading. Al-Sam'ani glosses the verb as roast him, and al-Biqa'i describes repeated immersion in the fire, like a sheep being roasted again and again. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy identify the man as Abu Jahl, while al-Dahhak and Muqatil name al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad, and some extend the warning to anyone of his kind. There is agreement that the fire is Hell and that the passage concerns disbelievers, while the commentators differ on the identity of the individual and the details of the scene.

This verse describes the fate of the one who is given his record in his left hand on the Day of Resurrection: he laments what he neglected, and God then commands the guardians to seize him, bind his hand to his neck, cast him into the Blazing Fire, and thread him onto a chain seventy cubits long. The commentators agree that the number seventy expresses length and intensity rather than an exact measure. The reason for the punishment follows: he did not believe in the Mighty God and did not urge the feeding of the needy. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others explain 'my authority has perished from me' as the loss of his proofs, while Ibn Zayd understands it as the loss of worldly rule and power, a view that Tabari and Ibn Kathir also associate with a man of standing. On the cubit, some say it is the king's cubit, as reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Juraij, others the ordinary known cubit, and al-Hasan says only God knows which one is meant. On how the chain is threaded, Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak report that it enters through the back and exits through the mouth or nostrils, while others say it coils around the body until it constricts it; no view is preferred. Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi observe that placing the chain and the Blaze first signals exclusivity and terror, and that 'then' indicates a gradation in severity rather than a delay, whereas Abu Hayyan allows that it may denote an interval. The ghislin, the food of the damned, is explained as the pus of the people of the Fire, a tree they eat, or the discharge from their bodies; all agree that only the sinners, that is the disbelievers, eat it.

This verse states that the one who receives his record in his left hand will be punished in the hereafter, and gives two reasons: he did not believe in Allah the Mighty, and he did not urge the feeding of the needy. Most commentators read the first clause as the cause of the punishment just described. Al-Tabari explains it as disbelief in Allah's oneness, while al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud note that calling God 'the Mighty' signals that greatness belongs to Him alone, so whoever claims it for himself deserves the harshest penalty. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as neglecting God's rights, such as worship and obedience. Al-Razi links the first clause to a corrupted rational faculty and the second to a corrupted practical faculty.

There is broad agreement that failing to urge the feeding of the poor is a grave fault, since the verse places it alongside disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur take it as a warning to believers to give the poor their due from their wealth, and Ibn 'Ashur observes that the implied criticism of stinginess is stronger than the famous poetic image of hospitality. Abu al-Darda' used to urge his wife to make more broth for the poor. Sayyid Qutb presents compassion for the needy as a fruit of faith.

The meaning of 'ghislin' is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas took it to be the pus of the damned, al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said it is a tree in hell, and Yahya ibn Sallam described it as the runoff from their bodies.

This verse describes the fate of the one who receives his record in his left hand. The commentators explain that in the world he did not urge people to feed the needy, and that in the Hereafter he will have no food except ghislin. They agree that refusing to feed the poor, and not encouraging others to do so, is a grave sin. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that this withholding is linked to disbelief, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that mentioning the failure to urge rather than the act itself shows that someone who does not urge is already blameworthy, and so much more one who does not act. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan add that the poor have a right in the wealth of the rich.

Scholars differ on the meaning of some words. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir understand hamim as a close relative or friend who would protect and help, whereas Muhammad ibn al-Mustanir takes it to mean boiling water. Regarding ghislin, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it to be the pus of the people of the Fire, Dahhak and Rabi' say it is a tree the people of the Fire eat, and Qatada describes it as the most vile of foods. Ibn Zayd says no one truly knows what it is. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify the khati'un as the disbelievers, while Abu Hayyan distinguishes the one who sins deliberately from the one who errs without intent. Some readers also note the recitation variants of the word.

This verse states that the one given his record in his left hand will have no close friend on the Day of Judgment who can help him or shield him from punishment. The commentators explain hamim as a near relative or friend who is moved by his plight and protects him, as al-Tabari reports from Ibn Zayd, while Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi stress that his kinsmen will rather shun him and flee from him. Ibn Abbas and others say that hamim here means boiling water, so the sense would be that he will have neither water nor food except the ghislin. On the meaning of ghislin there is wide agreement that it is the pus and fluids flowing from the bodies of the people of the Fire. Ibn Abbas and Ikrima describe it as blood and water flowing from their flesh, al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' say it is a tree they eat, Qatada calls it the worst and most loathsome food, and Ibn Zayd says that no one knows what it is. Yahya ibn Salam describes it as the washings of their insides, and Ibn Qutayba as a noun derived from the root of washing. Al-Qurtubi reports that some linguists take it to be what flows from a washed wound. Scholars also debate whether the ghislin and the dari' of Surat al-Ghashiya are the same thing or two distinct foods. The khati'un, the sinners, are understood as disbelievers by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir, as wrongdoers by al-Qurtubi, and as those who overstep truth for falsehood by al-Zamakhshari.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of the one who is given his record in his left hand on the Day of Resurrection: he has no close friend to protect him, and his only food is al-ghislin. For most of them this word means the pus and fluids that flow from the bodies of the damned. Al-Tabari reports from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Qatada that it is the worst and most repulsive food, and Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy give the same sense. Ibn Abbas is reported to have said he did not know what al-ghislin is and suspected it was al-zaqqum, while Dahhak and al-Rabi ibn Anas describe it as a tree that the people of the Fire eat. As for the "sinners" at the end of the verse, most identify them as disbelievers and polytheists, though al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi also keep the sense of those who overstep truth for falsehood. On the word hamim, most take it to mean a friend or close relative, whereas Muhammad ibn al-Mustanir understands it as hot water, meaning he will have no water or liquid at all. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi observe that taam means what is prepared to be eaten, and that the word may be used figuratively. Some connect al-ghislin with the dari' of Surat al-Ghashiya, while others hold that they are two different foods for two different groups of the damned.

This verse describes the fate of the one given his record in his left hand: on that day he has no close friend to help him or to ward off the punishment, and his only food is ghislin, the pus and discharge that flows from the bodies of the damned. The commentators agree that the sinners (al-khati'un) are those who commit wrongdoing deliberately, and they mostly identify them as polytheists and disbelievers. On the meaning of ghislin, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to be the pus of the people of the Fire, while Qatada and Ibn Zayd describe it as the worst and most loathsome food, and al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas say it is a tree the people of the Fire eat. Some, such as al-Tabari citing Basran grammarians, derive it from the word for washing and the flow from wounds, and al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi treat it as a noun of the form fi'lin from the root for washing. As for hamim, al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy understand it as a close relative or friend, whereas Muhammad ibn al-Mustanir takes it to mean boiling water, a view Ibn 'Atiyya reports without deciding. Regarding the recitation al-khati'un, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan record variant readings, and Abu Hayyan notes that Ibn 'Abbas rejected some of them while accepting the sense of those who transgress the truth. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di point out that failing to urge the feeding of the poor is placed alongside disbelief, which underlines its gravity.

God swears by everything that is seen and everything that is not seen, and most commentators read this oath as embracing all of creation. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Zayd and Ibn Abbas, speaks of all things, while Ibn Kathir sees in them signs of divine power; al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that everything divides into the perceptible and the imperceptible, which includes the Creator and creation, this world and the hereafter, bodies and spirits. On the particle 'la' at the start, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take it as a rejection of what the polytheists say or as a mere emphatic particle, whereas others read it as a negation of the oath, since the truth needs no swearing to be evident. As for the 'noble messenger', most, including Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, identify Muhammad ﷺ who conveys God's word, while al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba, in one report, name Gabriel. The verse denies that the Quran is the speech of a poet or a soothsayer. On the phrase 'little do you believe' and 'little do you remember', al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain that 'little' here means none at all. The passage concludes that the Quran is a revelation sent down from the Lord of the worlds.

God swears by everything that can be seen and everything that cannot be seen. The commentators explain that this covers all of creation: this world and the hereafter, bodies and spirits, humans and jinn, angels. Mujahid and others take it as a general oath. The Quraysh had accused the Prophet of being a sorcerer, a poet or a soothsayer, and the verse answers that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger who conveys it. The commentators disagree on who this messenger is. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take it to be Muhammad, while al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba take it to be Gabriel. Al-Razi adds that the Qur'an may be called God's speech, Gabriel's and Muhammad's, each in its own sense. The verse denies that the Qur'an is the speech of a poet or a soothsayer. Scholars differ on the word 'little' in 'little do you believe': al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan say it means not at all, while others keep its literal sense. Ibn Kathir also relates the story of Umar's conversion after hearing this surah. The passage concludes that the Qur'an is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.

God swears by all that is seen and all that is unseen that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger, meaning its recitation and delivery from God. Commentators differ on who this noble messenger is. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, identify him as the Prophet Muhammad, pointing to the context that denies him poetry and divination. Others, such as al-Kalbi, Muqatil, Ibn Qutayba and al-Hasan, identify him as Gabriel, who conveys the message from God. Al-Razi distinguished this verse from a similar one in Surat al-Takwir, where the same phrase refers to Gabriel, and concluded that here it refers to the Prophet. All agree that the Qur'an is God's speech and that attributing it to the messenger reflects his role in conveying it. God then rejects the Quraysh's charges of being a poet or a soothsayer, and al-Tabari traces these charges to their misunderstanding of the Qur'an. On the phrase "little do you believe", al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Qayyim read "little" as complete denial, meaning they do not believe at all, while others take it as genuine but meagre faith. Ibn Ashur notes that the description "noble" is enough to exclude madness and lying, and that poets and soothsayers were regarded as people of honour among the Arabs, which is why these two were singled out.

God swears by all that is seen and all that is unseen, then affirms that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger, not the words of a poet as the disbelievers claimed. The commentators agree that the Qur'an plainly differs from poetry. The word "qalilan" (little) in "little do you believe" is understood by al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan as a total negation: they do not believe at all. Ibn 'Atiyya suggests that "ma" may be negating, which yields the same meaning, or may be a verbal noun, meaning their faith is only slight, such as believing in some simple truths. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir and Ya'qub read the verb in the third person, while most read it in the second person.

The commentators differ on who the "noble messenger" is. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan identify him as the Prophet Muhammad, while al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba identify him as Gabriel, with Ibn Qutayba explaining that the Qur'an is God's word conveyed by the messenger. Al-Alusi holds that the context of revelation supports the reference to the Prophet. As for "what you do not see", some take it to mean angels or spirits, others the secrets of divine power. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that the Qur'an is neither poetry nor a soothsayer's speech, since it resembles neither verse nor the sayings of diviners inspired by demons. Ibn Kathir also relates the account of 'Umar's conversion upon hearing these verses.

God swears by everything that people see and everything they do not see that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger, meaning his recitation and proclamation, and that it is neither the speech of a poet nor the speech of a soothsayer. The commentators explain that the stress on the scarcity of faith and reflection among the audience is what drives them to such claims. They agree that the oath covers all creation, and that denying poetry and soothsaying means clearing the Prophet ﷺ of both, in answer to the accusations of the Quraysh. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take the word 'little' as meaning none at all: they neither believe nor reflect. Al-Tabari reads it as a weak faith. Ibn 'Atiyya considers that 'ma' may be a negation or a verbal particle. On the identity of the noble messenger, most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, name Muhammad ﷺ, while al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba name Gabriel, since the Qur'an is God's speech delivered through a messenger. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur see the description as honouring the Prophet. The commentators describe soothsaying as rhymed, often deceitful prose about uncertain matters, unlike the Qur'an in its order and meaning. The verse ends by affirming that the Qur'an is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.

This verse states that the Quran is a revelation sent down from the Lord of the worlds, meaning the speech of God delivered to His Messenger, not the composition of a poet or the utterance of a soothsayer as the disbelievers claimed. The commentators agree that its plain meaning is clear and needs no special interpretation, and that it confirms what precedes it: the Quran is the word of a noble messenger. They differ, however, on who that messenger is. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to be the Prophet Muhammad, while Ibn Qutayba and others, including al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi in one reading, identify him as Gabriel, the Quran being God's speech which the Prophet conveyed. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain that the attribution to the messenger reflects his role as one who faithfully delivers a message he did not originate. Some readers, such as Abu al-Sammal, read the word as an accusative, implying a hidden verb meaning he sent it down as a sending. The commentators note that the title "Lord of the worlds" points to the universal scope of God's lordship over all creation. The verse contains no legal ruling, and its meaning is drawn from the context of the verses around it.

This verse states that if the Prophet had invented sayings and attributed them to God, God would have seized him at once and cut his lifeline. The commentators agree that al-watin is a vein linked to the heart whose severing brings death quickly. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes take it as the sinew of the heart, al-Mujahid as the cord along the spine, Muhammad ibn Ka'b as the heart and what surrounds it, and al-Kalbi as a vein between the neck tendons and the throat. On the phrase "We would have taken him by the right hand", al-Farra', al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba read it as force and power, since the strength of everything lies on its right side; al-Hasan takes it as cutting off the right hand; al-Suddi and al-Hakam read it as truth; al-Tabari reads it as an image of humiliation, like a ruler ordering a man to be taken by the hand. Al-Zamakhshari pictures a public execution in which the executioner seizes the right hand of the condemned. The commentators note that the verse serves as evidence that the Quran comes from God, since the Prophet was not punished. Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani explain that "hajizin" means preventing, and that the plural is used because "ahad" in negation covers a group. All see the Quran as a reminder for the God-fearing and a cause of regret for the disbelievers, and read "haqq al-yaqin" as absolute certainty; the surah ends with the command to glorify the name of God.

This verse states that if the Prophet had invented sayings and attributed them to God, God would have seized him by force and cut his watin, the vein of the heart whose severing brings death. The commentators agree on the general meaning: a threat of immediate punishment for anyone who fabricates speech against God, and thus a proof that the Prophet was truthful, since God did not punish him. On the phrase 'by the right hand' they differ. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Farra', al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba take it to mean power and might, since, as Ibn Qutayba says, the strength of everything lies on its right side. Al-Hasan al-Basri understood it as the cutting off of the right hand, and al-Tabari favoured the sense of humiliation, like a ruler ordering a man's hand to be seized for punishment. Al-Zamakhshari explained that seizing by the right hand depicts a particularly dreadful public execution. As for the watin, Ibn Abbas and most exegetes say it is the vein attached to the heart, Mujahid says it is the cord along the spine, Muhammad ibn Ka'b says it is the heart and what surrounds it, and al-Kalbi says it is a vein between the neck tendon and the throat. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya note that 'hajizin' is plural because 'ahad' carries a collective sense. On 'haqq al-yaqin', the Kufans see an idafa of a thing to itself, while the Basrans and al-Mubarrad read it as the most complete certainty. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes three degrees of certainty: knowledge, sight and direct experience. Some report that this verse is recited in bowing, though Malik disliked making it obligatory lest it be treated as a required rite.

This passage of Surat al-Haqqa states that if the Prophet ﷺ had invented sayings and attributed them to God, God would have seized him at once with His power and cut his watin, the vessel linked to the heart whose severing brings death. The commentators largely agree on the meaning of watin: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes, following Ibn Abbas, take it to be the heart's sinew, while Mujahid says it is the cord along the spine, Muhammad ibn Ka'b the heart and what surrounds it, and al-Kalbi a vein between the neck muscles and the throat. On the phrase 'seized by the right hand', opinions differ. Ibn Abbas, al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj read it as power and might, al-Hasan as the cutting off of the right hand, and al-Tabari as a figure of humiliation, like a ruler ordering that a man's hand be taken to disgrace him. Al-Zamakhshari sees a terrifying image of execution by beheading. From the passage the commentators draw proof that the Qur'an comes from God, since God does not leave unpunished one who invents a lie in His name. The plural 'hajizin' agrees with the sense of 'ahad', which after a negation covers the whole group. They also agree that the Qur'an is a reminder for the pious and a cause of regret for the disbelievers, and they differ on 'haqq al-yaqin': the Kufans see an annexation of a thing to itself, while the Basrans read it as pure or complete certainty.

This verse states that if the Prophet had invented sayings and attributed them to God, God would have seized him at once, and no one among people could prevent that punishment. The commentators agree that "seizing by the right hand" means seizing with power or in humiliation, and that the "watin" is the vein or cord linked to the heart whose severing brings death. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes take it to be the nerve from which the heart is suspended, while Mujahid says it is the cord along the spine and Muhammad ibn Ka'b says it is the heart and what surrounds it. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the right hand as a public execution meant to shame, al-Tabari reads it as contempt, and Ibn Kathir gives the sense of strength.

All agree that the Qur'an is a reminder for the God-fearing and that rejecting it will be a source of regret for the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Mawardi adds that the regret may also be felt in this world, when they fail to match it. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan suggest the pronoun may refer to the rejection itself.

On the phrase "haqq al-yaqin", the Kufans see an annexation of a thing to itself, while the Basrans and al-Mubarrad read it as meaning perfect certainty. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes three degrees of certainty: knowledge, sight, and direct experience. The surah ends with a command to glorify the name of the Lord, which Ibn 'Abbas takes to mean prayer and others take to mean declaring God free of every flaw.

This verse states that the Quran is a reminder and an admonition specifically for the God-conscious, meaning those who fear God's punishment, perform His obligations and avoid what He forbids. The commentators link it to the passage in which God rejects the claim that the Prophet forged the Quran: had he invented sayings against Him, God would have seized him and no one could have held back the punishment. Most exegetes take the pronoun 'it' to refer to the Quran, although some, as al-Tabari reports, take it to refer to the Prophet. Al-Mawardi lists four possible meanings of 'reminder': mercy, steadfastness, admonition and deliverance, whereas al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir restrict it to admonition. On the phrase 'truth of certainty', the Kufans regard it as an idafa of a thing to itself, while the Basrans, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya read it as 'the pure, utter certainty'. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes three degrees of certainty: knowledge, seeing with the eye, and experiencing the truth directly. All agree that the verse warns the disbelievers, who will feel regret on the Day of Resurrection for having rejected the Quran, though they differ on whether the address is to people in general or to the believers alone.

This verse states that God knows that some among mankind will deny the Qur'an, and that this denial will become a source of regret for them. The commentators agree that it is a warning to those who reject the message: God knows them and will requite them for their refusal. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the regret (hasra) will come on the Day of Resurrection, when the disbelievers see the reward of those who believed. Al-Mawardi notes that it may also appear in this world, when the disbelievers were unable to produce anything like the Qur'an despite its challenge. Ibn 'Ashur stresses the contrast between the Qur'an's effect on the God-fearing and its effect on the disbelievers, two sides of the same message. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy report that some read the address as aimed at the believers, announcing that some of them would later disbelieve, a view also mentioned by Alusi. Al-Razi, by contrast, draws from the verse that the denial comes from people who prefer the pleasures of this world, and concludes that refusal is a human responsibility, a point the Mu'tazilites might invoke. Qurtubi adds that the denial may refer to the Qur'an or to the Prophet, according to the authors. These explanations agree on the general sense while leaving open several questions about the timing and the addressees of the regret.

This verse, within Surah al-Haqqa, states that the Quran is a source of anguish for the disbelievers. Commentators explain that they will feel this regret on the Day of Resurrection when they see the reward of the believers, as al-Tabari reports and Ibn Kathir repeats. Al-Mawardi adds that the regret may also be felt in this world, when they are unable to match the Quran despite the challenge it poses to them.

Most exegetes take the pronoun to refer to the Quran. Ibn Kathir notes that it may also refer to belief in it, which would then be a genuine regret for the disbelievers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Qatada that the hasra concerns denying the Quran. Al-Razi, citing Muqatil, holds that the pronoun refers to the denial itself, and al-Alusi judges the first reading more apparent.

Regarding the phrase haqq al-yaqin, Ibn Juzayy reports the view of the Kufans, for whom it is an annexation of a thing to itself, and that of the Basrans, who see the annexation of the strongest aspect of the truth. Al-Zamakhshari offers the equivalent of "the very certainty," and Ibn al-Qayyim describes three levels of certainty: knowledge of certainty, sight of certainty, and truth of certainty, which he links to direct experience.

This verse declares that the Qur'an is the absolute truth, a certainty with no doubt in it. The commentators explain that the phrase haqq al-yaqin has been read in different ways. The Kufans took it as an annexation of a thing to itself, while al-Mubarrad, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as meaning the purest or the perfect certainty. The Basrans and the most skilled scholars held that the word truth is annexed to the most complete of its qualities. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Sa'di describe three levels of certainty: knowledge of certainty, sight of certainty, and the truth of certainty, which comes from direct experience. As for the pronoun, most commentators refer it to the Qur'an, while Muqatil refers it to the act of denying it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that denying it will be a deep regret for the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment when they see the reward of the believers, and Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tha'alibi add that this regret may also be felt in this world when the deniers cannot match the Qur'an. On the final command to glorify the name of the Lord, Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean prayer, while others took it to mean declaring God free of all unfitting qualities. Al-Jaza'iri reports that it was ordered to be recited in bowing, and Malik disliked making this obligatory.

This closing verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to glorify the name of his Lord, the Great, at the end of the surah's argument that the Quran is true and that Muhammad did not invent it. Al-Tabari sees it as the conclusion of this discussion, and Ibn Kathir describes the Lord as the One who sent down this great Quran.

The commentators agree on the general meaning: to glorify God is to declare Him free of every imperfection while mentioning His great name. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi specify that this is saying "Glory be to God", and al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi stress purifying Him from every flaw. As-Sam'ani notes that the name and the one named are the same.

They differ on how the glorification should be understood. Ibn Abbas, quoted by al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and al-Tha'alibi, reads it as prayer: pray to your Lord. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take it as thanks for the revelation received, while al-Razi offers both thanks and a declaration that God is far above being credited with lies. Al-Qasimi reads it as steadfastness in the remembrance of God and in calling to Him alone, and Ibn 'Ashur understands the glorification as spoken praise.

Ibn 'Atiyya reports a narration that the Prophet said to place this verse in the bowing posture, and notes that some scholars recommended doing so, while Malik disliked making it binding so that it would not be treated as obligatory.
